407.title: Great by hearsay
407.hook: suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe: everyone calls You great from hearing, but only one who has seen knows (Asa, ang 9)
407.howItsDone: Suni vaddaa is the second shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; some Sikh teachers draw from it the reading that hearing about the Divine is a beginning, and knowing for oneself is the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, so dar, and your line, the door at dusk. Today, the second shabad of Rehras, and an honest question about how we know anything.

A boy from a village far inland grows up hearing about the sea. His uncle has been. The ocean is huge, the uncle says, bigger than all of Punjab, salty, loud, it never stops moving. The boy repeats it to his friends: the sea is huge. He's right. But he doesn't know it. Years later, he steps off a bus on the coast and walks to the edge of the water, and he goes completely quiet. He never says the sea is huge again.
screen: `A BOY WHO HAS HEARD ABOUT THE SEA.` → `HE REPEATS IT: THE SEA IS HUGE.` → `THEN HE SEES IT, AND GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: The second shabad of Rehras, Guru Nanak again, in Raag Asa, begins: suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe. Hearing, everyone calls You great. And then, in paraphrase: but how great You are, only someone who has seen can say. That's a startling way to open an evening prayer. It admits that talk about God can be hearsay: things we were told and repeated, secondhand. Guru Nanak doesn't mock it. Everyone says You're great, and they're right. But hearing is not the same as seeing. Then the shabad does something even more honest. It says those who did see couldn't describe it either. Your worth can't be estimated, it says, and can't be spoken. Those who tried to describe You were absorbed into You. The refrain calls out: my great Master, deep and profound, an ocean of virtue, nobody knows how vast You are. All the meditators met and meditated, it says; all the appraisers met and appraised; the scholars and teachers tried; and none of them could tell even a sliver. So the shabad leaves us between two things. Hearsay isn't enough, and seeing leaves you speechless. Like the boy at the sea. Some readers set this beside the Japji's suniai pauris: hearing as a real beginning, and seeing, knowing for yourself, as where the path goes. For the evening, the question is simple. What, today, did you actually see, not just hear about? Seen, not heard.
screen: `SUNI VADDAA: GREAT, FROM HEARING.` · `ONLY ONE WHO HAS SEEN CAN SAY.` · `THOSE WHO SAW WERE LEFT SPEECHLESS.` · `HEARING BEGINS; SEEING IS THE PATH.` · then, large: `SEEN, NOT HEARD.`

segments.voice: Find one thing from today or yesterday that you saw or felt for yourself, a kindness, a sky, a moment of peace, a fear that passed: not something you read about, something you were there for. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, I saw, I felt, and sit with it quietly, the way the boy stood at the water. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once.
Suni vaddaa, hearing, great: everyone calls the Lord great from hearing; only one who has seen knows, and even they can't describe it.
Your line: seen, not heard. Hearing is where it begins, not where it ends. That's today.

408.title: Remembering, I live
408.hook: aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao: chanting I live, forgetting I die (Asa, ang 9)
408.howItsDone: Aakhaa jeevaa is the third shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; remembering the Name, simran, through the day is central to Sikh practice, and some Sikhs repeat Waheguru quietly while they work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suni vaddaa, and your line, seen, not heard. Today, the third shabad of Rehras, and it's about forgetting.

A busy day. Meetings back to back, errands, messages. Somewhere around noon you meant to eat and didn't. By four o'clock you're snapping at people, the screen is blurry, everything feels harder than it should. And then it hits you: I forgot lunch. You weren't failing at life. You'd just forgotten the thing that keeps you going, and the cost showed up everywhere else. Tonight's shabad reaches for hunger too.
screen: `A BUSY DAY. LUNCH FORGOTTEN.` → `BY FOUR, EVERYTHING IS HARDER.` → `OH. I FORGOT TO EAT.`

segments.voice: The third shabad of Rehras, Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, opens with this line: aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao. Saying it, I live; forgetting, I die. It, here, is the Name. Then, straight away, honesty: it's hard to say the True Name. Not hard to pronounce. Hard to keep saying, to keep remembering, through a day full of everything else. And then the hunger picture. If a person feels hunger for the True Name, the shabad says in paraphrase, that hunger eats up their pain. That's a reversal. Usually hunger is the problem. Here, the right hunger is the cure: wanting the Name so much that the wanting itself consumes sorrow. The refrain asks: so kio visrai meree maae. How could I forget Him, my mother? You've heard that address before: meree maae, my mother, is how the Anand began. Here it's a plea, almost a worry: how could I ever forget? The shabad goes on to say that even if everyone gathered to praise Him, He wouldn't grow greater, and if no one did, He wouldn't grow less. He doesn't die, and there's no mourning for Him; He keeps on giving, and His gifts never run out. So remembering isn't for His sake. It's for ours. The remembering is the lunch. Forget it, and by four o'clock the whole soul is running on empty. Remember, and live.
screen: `AAKHAA JEEVAA: SAYING IT, I LIVE.` · `IT'S HARD TO KEEP SAYING THE NAME.` · `HUNGER FOR THE NAME EATS PAIN.` · `HOW COULD I FORGET, MY MOTHER?` · then, large: `REMEMBER AND LIVE.`

segments.voice: Let the day's noise settle, then gently remember: if you pray, say Waheguru once, slowly, and let it be the meal you skipped; if you don't, hold the one thing that keeps you going, a person, a purpose, a quiet you trust. When the mind wanders back into the day, that's forgetting; notice it, and remember again.
Remembering. Aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao: saying the Name, I live; forgetting it, I die. The third shabad of Rehras, by Guru Nanak.
Your line: remember and live. The remembering is for us, not for Him. See you tomorrow.

409.title: So Purakh: that Being
409.hook: so purakh niranjan: that Being is pure, beyond reach, and all meditate on Him (Asa M4, ang 10–11)
409.howItsDone: So Purakh is the first of four shabads in the second group of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; in kirtan it can be sung slowly, its doubled phrases repeated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering, and your line, remember and live. Today, a second group of shabads inside Rehras, and a new voice.

Kajal, the black eyeliner, can be made at home by an old method. You light a small oil lamp and hold a clay or brass plate just above the flame. In a few minutes the underside is coated in soft black soot. Scrape it off, mix it with a little ghee, and you have kajal. The flame itself stays bright and clean. Everything it touches turns black. That old word for soot and eyeliner, anjan, is hiding inside today's line.
screen: `A PLATE HELD OVER A LAMP.` → `SOOT: THE OLD WAY TO MAKE KAJAL.` → `THE FLAME STAYS CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Rehras has two more shabads in its first group, and we'll come back to them in a few days. Today we jump to the second group, called So Purakh after its opening words. The voice changes too. These are by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru. It opens: so purakh niranjan. That Being, purakh, is niranjan. Nir means without. Anjan is that soot, the black of kajal, and so a stain. Niranjan: without a stain. Untouched by the soot of the world, the way the flame stays clean while the plate turns black. The line goes on: the Lord, beyond reach, beyond reach, without limit. Then, in paraphrase: all meditate on You, all meditate on You, true Creator. All beings are Yours, and You are the giver to every being. Meditate on the Lord, saints; He takes away every sorrow. And then a line that turns everything inward: the Lord Himself is the master, and the Lord Himself is the servant. What is poor Nanak? Guru Ram Das signs with the name Nanak, as the Gurus whose hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib do. Notice the repeating. Beyond reach, beyond reach. All meditate, all meditate. The words circle, the way a lamp flame flickers but stays a flame. In kirtan, So Purakh can be sung slowly, the lines doubling back. The picture it leaves at dusk is simple: whatever soot the day has left on you, that Being is untouched by it. Pure being.
screen: `SO PURAKH: GURU RAM DAS'S SHABADS.` · `NIRANJAN: WITHOUT A STAIN, NO SOOT.` · `ALL MEDITATE ON YOU, GIVER OF ALL.` · `HIMSELF THE MASTER, HIMSELF THE SERVANT.` · then, large: `PURE BEING.`

segments.voice: Say so purakh niranjan three times, slowly, out loud or under your breath. Then let the words go and picture a lamp flame, steady and clean while the plate above it gathers soot, and let the day's smudges be on the plate, not the flame. If you pray, you can end with Waheguru.
So Purakh. That Being: the opening of Guru Ram Das's shabads in Rehras. So purakh niranjan: that Being is without stain, beyond reach, the giver of all.
Your line: pure being. Nir, without; anjan, the soot of the lamp. Day four hundred nine, done.

410.title: You are the true Creator
410.hook: too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee: You are the true Creator, my Master (Asa M4, ang 11)
410.tomorrow: A pool of fire and water
410.howItsDone: Too kartaa sachiaar is the second shabad of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its line that the Lord is the river within which all things are is often quoted in Sikh teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, So Purakh, and your line, pure being. Today, Guru Ram Das's second shabad, and it speaks straight to the Maker.

Pick up a handmade bowl at a craft fair and turn it over. On the bottom, pressed into the clay, there's often a little mark: initials, a symbol, the potter's stamp. The bowl doesn't know it's there. It just holds soup. But the mark says someone shaped this, on purpose, with their hands. Guru Ram Das looks at a whole day that way: the light this morning, the people in it, the breath you're breathing now. Tonight's shabad turns the day over and reads the mark.
screen: `A HANDMADE BOWL, TURNED OVER.` → `THE POTTER'S MARK ON THE BASE.` → `TONIGHT: READ THE MARK ON THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The second So Purakh shabad, by Guru Ram Das, opens: too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee. You are the true Creator, my Master. Kartaa is the maker, the same word as in the Mool Mantar's karta purakh. Sachiaar is true. And maiddaa saanee, my Master, is said in western Punjabi forms, the speech of the plains around Multan, so even the grammar sounds like someone talking at home. Then, in paraphrase: whatever pleases You comes to pass; whatever You give, that is what I receive. All belongs to You, and all meditate on You. The one You bless receives the jewel of the Name. The shabad gives the two directions a person can face: the gurmukh, turned toward the Guru, finds it; the manmukh, turned toward the self, loses it. Then come two pictures. You Yourself separate us, the shabad says, and You Yourself bring us together. And: You are the river, and everything is within You; without You, there is no other. All beings are Your play. So the Maker isn't standing outside the day, like a potter who walked away from the wheel. The Maker is the river the whole day flows in. For Sikhs saying Rehras, that changes what thank you means at dusk: not thanks sent off to a distant address, but the bowl noticing the hands still holding it. And the closing note is trust, said simply: You are my Master.
screen: `TOO KARTAA SACHIAAR: YOU ARE THE TRUE MAKER.` · `WHAT YOU GIVE IS WHAT I RECEIVE.` · `GURMUKH FINDS, MANMUKH LOSES.` · `YOU ARE THE RIVER; ALL IS IN YOU.` · then, large: `MY MASTER.`

segments.voice: Turn today over, like the bowl, and find three things you didn't make yourself: the morning light, someone who cooked or drove or helped, the breath itself. Give each one a quiet thank you; if you pray, you can use the shabad's own words, too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee, or simply Waheguru. Then rest.
Kartaa, the Maker: Guru Ram Das calls the Lord the true Maker and his Master, the river in which everything flows.
Your line: my master. Whatever You give, good or hard, is what I receive. Until tomorrow.

411.title: A pool of fire and water
411.hook: in the world's pool we dwell, where water and fire both are, feet stuck in the mud of attachment (Asa M1, ang 12)
411.tomorrow: This human body is your chance
411.howItsDone: This shabad is the third of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; Sikh teachers cite its closing line when explaining the place of sangat, the company of those who remember, in Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kartaa, the Maker, and your line, my master. Tonight's shabad is darker, and very honest.

Monsoon in a Punjabi village. The field path has turned to thick brown mud. You step off the bricks, and your foot sinks to the ankle. You pull. The mud pulls back. You pull harder, and your foot comes out, without the shoe. Mud like that has a rule: the harder you yank, the tighter it holds. Guru Nanak pictures the world as a pool with mud like that.
screen: `MONSOON. A FIELD PATH TURNED TO MUD.` → `THE HARDER YOU PULL, THE TIGHTER IT HOLDS.` → `GURU NANAK SAW THE WORLD LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: The third So Purakh shabad is by Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa. It begins, in paraphrase: we live in that pool, and He made both water and fire there. A pool where water and fire live together: things that cool and things that burn, comfort and craving, side by side. Then the mud. In the mud of attachment, moh, the feet can't move. I have seen people drowning there. Moh is the clinging kind of love: to things, to status, to having it our way. It doesn't feel like a trap. It feels like the ground. Then the shabad turns to the mind: foolish mind, you don't remember the One. Forgetting the Lord, your virtues waste away. And then a turn. Guru Nanak doesn't present himself as the one standing safely on the bank. He says, in effect: I'm not a celibate ascetic, I'm not a model of virtue, I'm not learned. My life has been foolish and ignorant. Then the closing line: Nanak prays, I seek the shelter of those who have not forgotten You. So the way out of the mud isn't pulling harder on your own. It's reaching for a hand: the company of people who remember, the sangat. Not willpower alone, and not leaving the world behind. The shabad stays in the pool of fire and water, and reaches for those who remember. Out of the mud.
screen: `A POOL WHERE WATER AND FIRE LIVE.` · `MOH: THE MUD THAT HOLDS THE FEET.` · `NOT CELIBATE, NOT VIRTUOUS, NOT LEARNED.` · `SHELTER WITH THOSE WHO REMEMBER.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Lift your feet a little off the floor, wiggle your toes and feel how free they are, then set them down. Name one thing that's been holding your feet lately, a grudge, a habit, a worry you keep feeding, without yanking at it. Then think of one steady person who remembers, and picture taking their hand; if you pray, you can say Waheguru once.
Moh, attachment. Guru Nanak's picture of the world in Rehras: water and fire together, feet stuck in the mud of moh, and shelter with those who haven't forgotten the Lord.
Your line: out of the mud. Not by yanking harder, but by taking a hand. That's day four hundred eleven.

412.title: This human body is your chance
412.hook: bhaee paraapat maanukh dehureeaa: you have this human body; now is your chance (Asa M5, ang 12)
412.howItsDone: Bhaee paraapat is the last shabad of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its opening line is quoted in Sikh teaching about the preciousness of human life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moh, and your line, out of the mud. Tonight, the last So Purakh shabad, and it's about time.

A crowded government office. You took a paper ticket an hour ago: number 147. The screen says 139. You scroll your phone, check the time, scroll again. 143. You go to get water. 145. You answer a message from your cousin. And then you look up and the screen says 149, and a voice is calling a number that isn't yours anymore. Your turn came, and passed, while you were looking somewhere else. Guru Arjan uses that very idea, a turn.
screen: `TICKET 147. THE SCREEN SAYS 139.` → `SCROLLING, WATER, A MESSAGE.` → `THE SCREEN SAYS 149.`

segments.voice: The fourth So Purakh shabad is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. It opens: bhaee paraapat maanukh dehureeaa. You have received this human body. Then: gobind milan kee eh teree bareeaa. This is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe. Bareeaa is a turn, like a turn in a queue, or your turn at the well. Sikh teaching speaks of the soul passing through many lives, and of a human birth as rare and precious, the one in which a person can consciously remember the One. So the shabad says, in paraphrase: other work won't help you here. Join the company of the holy and meditate on the Name alone. Put your effort into crossing the frightening ocean of the world; your life is slipping away in the color of maya. Notice it doesn't say other work is evil. Sikhs work, raise families and run businesses; Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan building the Harmandir Sahib. It says other work can't do this particular job. Then, like Guru Nanak yesterday, Guru Arjan turns humble. I haven't practiced meditation, austerity, self-control or right living, he says. I haven't served the holy or known the Lord. Nanak says: my deeds are lowly. I have come to Your shelter; protect my honor. So the chance isn't something to earn by being impressive. It's a turn that's already come. The number on the screen is yours, right now. Now is the chance.

413.title: The humble plea
413.hook: the Lord's humble servants ask the True Guru for the Name (Gujri M4, ang 10)
413.howItsDone: Har ke jan satgur satpurkhaa is the fourth shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its line naming the Lord's praise as rahraas is often given as the source of the prayer's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maanukh, and your line, now is the chance. Today we step back to a shabad we skipped, and it holds the name of the whole prayer.

Some people find it easy to ask for help. Others would rather drive around lost for an hour than ask for directions. They say I'm fine, I've got it, don't worry about me, and then carry it alone. Asking can feel like admitting you're small. Guru Ram Das, a Guru the sangat bowed to, wrote a shabad that is nothing but asking, and calls himself very small indeed.
screen: `DRIVING LOST RATHER THAN ASKING.` → `I'M FINE, I'VE GOT IT.` → `A GURU'S SHABAD THAT ONLY ASKS.`

segments.voice: In Rehras, after the three shabads we heard a few days ago, come two more in Raag Gujri, before the So Purakh group. We're going back for them now. The first is by Guru Ram Das. It begins, in paraphrase: O servant of the Lord, True Guru, True Being, I make my plea to the Guru. We are worms and insects, True Guru, and we seek Your shelter. Be kind, and let the light of the Name shine. Worms and insects. Guru Ram Das was the fourth Guru, remembered in Sikh tradition as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar. And here he speaks as the smallest of creatures, asking. Then the refrain: my friend, divine Guru, light up the Lord's Name in me. And then a line you'll recognize. Through the Guru's teaching, the Name is the friend of my breath, and the Lord's praise is my rahraas: the very word the evening prayer is named for, provisions for the road. The shabad goes on: great is the fortune of the Lord's servants who have faith in Him and thirst for Him. So this is what a plea looks like in Sikh prayer. Not bargaining, not a list of demands. An honest admission of smallness, and a request for the one thing that matters: the Name. The word for it here is binau, a humble petition. It's the same spirit as Ardas, where Sikhs stand and ask, with folded hands. The humble ask.
screen: `TWO GUJRI SHABADS, BEFORE SO PURAKH.` · `WE ARE WORMS AND INSECTS; WE SEEK SHELTER.` · `THE LORD'S PRAISE IS MY RAHRAAS.` · `BINAU: A HUMBLE PETITION FOR THE NAME.` · then, large: `THE HUMBLE ASK.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been carrying alone, and of who could help: a friend, a sibling, a colleague, a doctor. If you pray, bring it to God first, in the plain words of your own heart, or say Waheguru once. Then picture asking, simply, could you help me with this, and notice what it feels like in your chest, and breathe through it.
Binau, a humble plea: Guru Ram Das asks the True Guru for the light of the Name. This week: hearsay, remembering, that Being, the true Creator, the muddy pool, your chance, and now the humble ask.
Your line: the humble ask. In this shabad, the asking is the prayer. A week, done.
